common_name: Cayuse Oat (Pacific Northwest Standard Cover Crop and Forage Oat)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast 3 bu/acre (about 3-4 lb/1000 sq ft) in late summer to fall for a winter-kill cover, or as early as ground is workable in spring; Cayuse's short, stiff straw resists lodging, making it a favored nurse crop for interseeded legumes and grasses.

directions: Cayuse was released by Washington State University in 1966 from a Craig/Alamo cross made at Cornell, and it remains one of the most widely sown oat cultivars in the Pacific Northwest for cover cropping, hay, and green chop. Its pale green, short, stiff straw resists lodging better than many older oat types, which makes it a reliable companion crop when establishing clovers or perennial grasses on irrigated ground. Drill or broadcast seed into a firm bed in fall for a winter-killed mulch that protects soil through the rainy season, or sow in early spring to build biomass and scavenge nitrogen ahead of a summer crop. Mow or crimp before seed set if used purely as a green manure to prevent volunteer regrowth.
sources: Oregon State University Forage Information System

common_name: Monida Oat (High-Yield Intermountain West Forage and Cover Crop Oat)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast 3 bu/acre (about 3-4 lb/1000 sq ft) as soon as soil can be worked in spring; Monida is a mid-to-late-season, high-yielding forage oat bred for the Intermountain West and works equally well as a fall-sown winter-kill cover in milder zones.

directions: Monida was released in 1984 from an Otana/Cayuse cross by USDA-ARS and the Idaho, Oregon, Washington, and Montana agricultural experiment stations, and it has become a popular high-yielding spring forage oat across the Intermountain West. It produces plump, short white kernels and good lodging resistance, with dry matter yields that exceed many older PNW oat varieties. Sow into a firm seedbed as soon as ground is workable for a fast, dense stand that suppresses weeds, protects bare soil from erosion, and scavenges residual nitrogen; mow or terminate before seed set if grown strictly as a green manure. In cold-winter zones it reliably winter-kills when fall-sown, leaving a protective mat of residue for no-till spring planting.

common_name: Otana Oat (Tall Blue-Green Intermountain Forage and Cover Crop Oat)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast 3 bu/acre (about 3-4 lb/1000 sq ft) as soon as soil can be worked; Otana is a tall, blue-green-foliaged mid-season oat, a parent of Monida, valued for dry hay, silage, grazing, and cleanup cover cropping after alfalfa.

directions: Otana was jointly released in 1976 by the Montana and Idaho Agricultural Experiment Stations from a CI5345/Zanster cross and remains a widely grown spring forage oat in irrigated and dryland areas of the Intermountain West. It is taller than Cayuse with distinctive blue-green foliage, moderate lodging resistance, and a higher test weight than many earlier PNW cultivars. Growers commonly use it to clean up fields coming out of alfalfa without losing a hay cutting, or as a fast-establishing cover crop that winter-kills reliably in cold-winter regions, leaving a weed-suppressing mat of residue. Broadcast or drill into a firm bed in early spring and mow or terminate before seed set if used purely as green manure.

common_name: Rushmore Oat (Modern South Dakota-Bred Forage and Cover Crop Oat)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast 3 bu/acre (about 3-4 lb/1000 sq ft) as soon as soil can be worked in spring; Rushmore is a medium-late, lodging-resistant oat released by South Dakota State University in 2021 and widely marketed for fast-establishing forage, food-plot, and cover crop stands.

directions: Rushmore was released in 2021 by South Dakota State University, bred for improved grain quality and better lodging resistance than the older Hayden variety while keeping strong yield potential. Its fast early growth and dense canopy make it a popular choice for quick-cover plantings that suppress weeds, reduce erosion, and scavenge nitrogen ahead of a following crop, and it performs especially well on sandy soils where many oats struggle. Broadcast or drill into a firm, moist seedbed in early spring, or sow in late summer to fall where a winter-killed residue mat is wanted ahead of no-till spring planting. Mow or terminate before seed set if grown strictly as a green manure rather than for grain or hay.

common_name: Chief Crimson Clover (Classic Early Reseeding Southern Cover Crop Clover)

planting.note: Broadcast 15-20 lb/acre (about 5-8 oz/1000 sq ft) onto a fine, firm seedbed in fall; Chief is one of the original USDA-released reseeding crimson clover cultivars, maturing about a week earlier than Kentucky Pride and Talladega.

directions: Chief is one of the earliest USDA-developed reseeding crimson clover cultivars, released alongside Dixie and Auburn in the mid-twentieth century as part of a Southern breeding effort to give crimson clover the ability to naturally reseed itself in pasture and cropland rotations. It fixes substantial nitrogen through fall and winter growth, then produces a dense flush of crimson blooms in spring that draw abundant pollinator activity before setting seed. Broadcast onto a firm, weed-free seedbed in early fall so plants can establish a strong root system before hard frost, and either mow at early bloom for maximum nitrogen release or allow a portion of the stand to set seed for a self-sustaining reseeding cover in future years. Terminate before pod shatter if seed carryover into a following crop is not wanted.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service — Plant Materials Program

common_name: Apache Arrowleaf Clover (Bean Yellow Mosaic Virus-Tolerant Texas Arrowleaf Clover)

planting.note: Broadcast 8-10 lb/acre onto a firm, well-drained seedbed between mid-September and mid-March in the Gulf South; Apache germinates slowly at first but was bred specifically for tolerance to bean yellow mosaic virus, a disease that had eroded stand reliability in older arrowleaf cultivars.

directions: Apache was released by the Texas Agricultural Experiment Station in 2001 after six cycles of selection from Yuchi, Meechee, and Amclo breeding lines, making it the first arrowleaf clover cultivar bred specifically for tolerance to bean yellow mosaic virus. Like other arrowleaf clovers it grows tall and upright with an arrow-shaped leaflet marking, fixes significant nitrogen over a long fall-to-spring growing season, and produces abundant white-to-pink flower heads that are highly attractive to pollinators. Broadcast onto a well-drained, well-prepared bed in early fall and cover lightly, since arrowleaf clover requires good drainage and performs poorly on wet, poorly drained ground. Mow or terminate at early bloom for maximum nitrogen release, or allow it to reseed naturally in upland pastures and orchard alleys.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Aggie Clover

common_name: Seaton Park Subterranean Clover (Persistent Black-Seeded Mid-Season Subclover)

planting.note: Broadcast 12-15 lb/acre onto a firm seedbed in early fall; Seaton Park is a black-seeded, mid-season subclover valued for persistence under dry springs and heavy grazing, and is naturalized in California vineyard and orchard cover systems.

directions: Seaton Park is a black-seeded, mid-season-flowering subterranean clover selected in Australia for its unusually strong persistence under grazing pressure and dry spring conditions, and it has since been evaluated and adopted in California orchard and vineyard cover-crop systems. Its moderately hard seed coat and higher level of hard seed than earlier subclovers give it better resilience through false-autumn germination events and short dry spells after emergence. Broadcast onto a firm, weed-free bed in early fall and rake in shallowly, since subclovers bury their own seed pods at the soil surface after flowering to create a low, self-reseeding living mulch. Mow to control height under trees and vines, and let a portion of the stand set seed each year so the planting persists without replanting.
sources: Sustainable Agriculture Research & Education Program (UC Davis SAREP)

common_name: Trikkala Subterranean Clover (Vigorous Winter-Active Yanninicum-Type Subclover)

planting.note: Broadcast 12-15 lb/acre onto a firm seedbed in early fall; Trikkala is a large-cream-seeded yanninicum-type subclover that produces roughly twice the January-February winter growth of other subclovers and is the only subterranean clover type that tolerates standing water or seasonal seepage.

directions: Trikkala belongs to the yanninicum subspecies of subterranean clover, distinguished by large cream-colored seed and by far the strongest tolerance of wet or seasonally waterlogged soil of any subclover type, making it useful on seepy orchard rows or low spots where Mt. Barker or Woogenellup would fail. It produces rapid, heavy winter growth that suppresses cool-season weeds quickly after fall establishment and fixes substantial nitrogen through a long fall-to-spring season. Broadcast onto a firm, moist bed in early fall and rake in shallowly; like other subclovers it buries its own seed pods after flowering, letting a self-reseeding stand persist for years. Mow periodically to control height and encourage tillering, and let a portion of the stand set seed each season to maintain the planting without reseeding by hand.
sources: Sustainable Agriculture Research & Education Program (UC Davis SAREP)
